audio.t: Attention, all students. The Computer and Network Center will hold a free cybersecurity workshop this Wednesday from two to four in the afternoon in Room three oh five of the Information Building. Seats are limited to sixty, so please register through the student portal by noon on Tuesday.

audio.t: Good afternoon, everyone. I'm Kevin Lin from the university's information security team. As the semester gets busier, we usually see a rise in scam messages, and this term is no exception. Last month alone, more than three hundred students received fake emails claiming that a tuition refund was waiting for them.

These messages can look very convincing. They use our school logo and sometimes even a real staff member's name. But there are a few warning signs. First, they create a sense of urgency, like, your account will be closed in twenty-four hours. Second, the sender's address doesn't end in our official school domain. And third, they ask you to click a link and log in.

Remember, our office will never ask for your password by email or by phone. If something looks suspicious, don't reply. Forward it to the security team's report address, which you can find on the IT homepage. And please turn on two-step verification before final exams start. It only takes about five minutes, and it's the single best way to protect your account.

questions.explain: 講者說明詐騙訊息增加、警訊特徵與處理方式，目的是教學生辨識與應對詐騙。A 的退費正是詐騙內容；B、D 未被談及。
options: To announce a tuition refund
To explain new exam rules
To help students recognize and handle scam messages
To introduce new IT staff members

options: Over three hundred students received fake refund emails.
The school changed its official logo.

The message contains spelling mistakes.

head: From: Computer and Network Center <cnc@university.edu.tw>
To: All Students
Subject: Required Password Update and Two-Step Verification
passage: Following several recent phishing attempts targeting our campus, all student accounts must be updated by December 10. After that date, accounts that have not been updated will be temporarily suspended until the owner visits our service desk in person.

To update your account, log in to the student portal yourself, choose a new password of at least twelve characters, and set up two-step verification using the school's authenticator app. The whole process takes less than ten minutes.

Please note that this email does not contain any links. If you receive a similar message that asks you to click a link to update your account, it is a scam. Do not respond, and report it to security@university.edu.tw.
Thank you for helping us keep our campus network safe.

questions.explain: 第二段說未更新的帳號 will be temporarily suspended until the owner visits our service desk in person。信中是「暫停」而非永久刪除，也沒有收費或自動改密碼。
options: They will be deleted permanently.
Their owners will be charged a fee.
Their passwords will be changed automatically.
They will be suspended until the student visits the service desk.
questions.prompt: What will happen to accounts that are not updated by December 10?

questions.explain: 第四段說若收到要求點連結更新帳號的信就是詐騙，藉此讓學生分辨真假通知。其他選項信中皆未提及。
options: To keep the message short
To help students tell real notices from fake ones
Because the student portal is currently down

ignoring
protecting

passage: Every November, as students start searching for winter break jobs, the campus Career Center receives a wave of worried visitors. This year, the center has already handled more than forty reports of fake job offers, almost twice as many as last year. Most of the offers were posted in student social media groups and promised high pay for "simple online tasks."

One junior in the Department of Economics, who asked not to be named, said she was offered NT$1,500 an hour to "review products" from home. After she agreed, the recruiter asked for a photo of her student ID and her bank account details so that she could "receive her salary." Two days later, she discovered that her account had been used to move money from other scam victims. "I thought I was earning extra pocket money," she said. "Instead, I ended up talking to the police."

According to Professor Huang Mei-ling, who teaches information law, students are attractive targets because they are often short of money and tend to trust messages shared by classmates. "Scammers know that a post in a familiar group feels safer than a random advertisement," she explained. She added that lending a bank account to strangers, even without knowing its purpose, can lead to serious legal trouble.

To reduce the risk, the Career Center now checks every company before listing its jobs on the official job board. Staff also recommend that students never pay a "training fee," never hand over bank cards or passwords, and search the company's name online before any interview. Students who are unsure about an offer can book a free fifteen-minute consultation at the center.

questions.explain: 全文從假工作通報倍增、學生受害案例、教授分析到職涯中心建議，主旨是學生求職詐騙增加與防範。A、B、D 皆非重點。
options: A new law on part-time work for students
How to write a strong resume for winter jobs
A rise in fake job offers aimed at students and how to avoid them
The most popular winter break jobs on campus
questions.prompt: What is the article mainly about?
